general.temas: Recurring technological failures and their effects on aviation and other services feature prominently, as do political moves by Democrats. Trump’s trip to Asia and the clash between Federal Reserve Governor Lisa Cook and the White House also appear. Only Los Angeles Times highlights the health emergency linked to a local landfill.
general.motivo_crispacion: Political tension is reflected in the investigations House Democrats are preparing into Trump and his circle, and in the challenge to Chuck Schumer’s leadership. There is also an institutional clash between Lisa Cook and the White House over a hearing on her possible removal. Technological failures and a lawsuit by Ecuadorian fishermen against the United States add to the concern and conflict. These stories are partially offset by others about health, travel, sports and entertainment.

The New York Times.resumen:
- Carney and Trump hold an unplanned trade meeting at an Asian summit; Trump also meets Imelda Marcos in Manila.
- Mary Peltola wins the Alaska Senate seat with a campaign focused on local issues.
- House Democrats prepare investigations into Trump as vote counts continue in three close elections.
- Digital failures and cybersecurity vulnerabilities worry hospitals and users; Rubio rules out cyberattacks as the cause of the recent failures.
- A study warns of potential harmful uses of AI; the front page also offers dessert ideas and a review of Grand Theft Auto VI.
The New York Times.motivo_populismo: The tone is predominantly informative, although expressions such as “if the country is falling apart” and the urgency surrounding cybersecurity vulnerabilities add drama; there is no apparent appeal to the people against the elites.
The New York Times.sesgo: The front page prioritizes US politics and technological risks, with attention to Democratic victories and investigations. The selection provided does not reveal a clear partisan position.

The Washington Post.resumen:
- A man is sentenced to 27 years in prison for a thwarted plot against US leaders, including Trump and Biden.
- Studies examine a leukemia vaccine, exercise during GLP-1 treatment and an allergy linked to ticks; there is also reporting on measles.
- Graduate students are increasingly turning to private loans amid limits on federal funding.
- Ecuadorian fishermen sue the US over a drone strike; another story addresses FAA oversight of a repair before an air traffic shutdown.
- A Federal Reserve governor refuses to attend a removal hearing; the front page also covers Thanksgiving travel and a public bath in Chicago.
The Washington Post.motivo_populismo: The headlines are mostly informative, although expressions such as “a year of breakthroughs” and “siren song” add emphasis; there is no apparent appeal to the people against the elites.
The Washington Post.sesgo: The selection pays attention to the accountability of US authorities and the effects of their decisions, alongside health, economic and everyday-life topics. The writing is mainly factual, although some stories highlight criticism of government agencies and public policies.

The Wall Street Journal.resumen:
- Several universities offer three-year degrees to reduce costs; disputes over grades and allegations of sexual assault are also covered.
- A hearing for a Navy nominee reveals the use of expired missiles in the war with Iran; another report visits a US aircraft carrier.
- Fed Governor Lisa Cook rejects a White House hearing; in Silicon Valley, a proposed tower stirs controversy.
- A New York police unit dedicated to protests is disbanded, and several educational institutions oppose a tax proposal concerning racial preferences.
- The front page includes stories about healthy habits and college sports, as well as Lindsay Clancy’s retrial over the deaths of her three children.
The Wall Street Journal.motivo_populismo: The tone is predominantly informative, although words such as “fight,” “force” and “obsessed” add drama; there is no apparent appeal to the people against the elites.
The Wall Street Journal.sesgo: The selection gives particular prominence to higher education and institutional and local conflicts. The coverage combines public affairs with stories about trends and incidents, with no clear political orientation apparent in the headlines.

Los Angeles Times.resumen:
- Technology and air traffic control failures cause alarm and flight cancellations; refund options are explained.
- California universities debate the return of the SAT; the state also restricts Waymo’s operations and demands data from plastic producers.
- A chemical leak at a Los Angeles-area landfill raises health concerns; a report provides details about the death of a student.
- Trump arrives in China for a planned summit with the leaders of China and Russia.
- Other stories cover store closures, cultural funding for the Los Angeles Games and hotel changes in Mendocino.
Los Angeles Times.motivo_populismo: Expressions such as “airport chaos,” “Explosive trash geyser” and “mad dash” add drama, but there is no apparent appeal to the people against the elites.
Los Angeles Times.sesgo: The selection prioritizes California and Los Angeles, with attention to local problems, regulation and effects on residents. Opposing positions are presented in the debate over the SAT.

New York Post.resumen:
- The US conducted a scheduled test of an unarmed intercontinental missile during Trump’s trip to Asia.
- Schumer says he has the votes needed to retain the Democratic leadership in the Senate.
- California home sales fall and a major KFC franchisee files for bankruptcy.
- The Dodgers and the Blue Jays compete to sign Tarik Skubal; the Yankees get Chase Hampton back.
- The front page includes stories about TV series, the new James Bond and a Netflix executive’s move to Paramount.
New York Post.motivo_populismo: There is sensationalism and emotional language, such as “on the verge of collapse” and “hits rock bottom,” but no apparent explicit appeal to the people against the elites.
New York Post.sesgo: The selection favors entertainment, sports and dramatic angles. The headline about Schumer takes a disparaging tone that contrasts with the description of his leadership dispute.

opiniones.comunista:
I see a warning in the digital breakdowns: a society that depends on complex systems cannot treat their maintenance as an afterthought. We do not know whether the failures are connected, but their effects extend to flights, banks and government agencies. I advocate publicly funded and democratically controlled infrastructure, with workers who have the resources to keep it safe.

Class struggle also appears in education: by limiting federal loans for graduate study, the government is pushing students toward private lenders. A social need is thus turned into a business opportunity. I would rather expand public funding and move toward collective ownership of essential services. It is not enough to correct the excesses of big capital: its power must be challenged so that the priorities of the working majority prevail over private profit.
opiniones.anarquista:
The digital failures that have affected flights, banks and public services remind me how vulnerable we are when we depend on systems that a few control and almost no one can examine. I do not know whether those failures are connected, but I do believe the answer cannot be to hand even more power to governments and big corporations. We need transparent infrastructure, overseen by those who use and maintain it, and local alternatives that allow us to help one another when systems fail.

I am also troubled that, as public funding for graduate study is reduced, more students are turning to private lenders. Exchanging dependence on the state for dependence on creditors is not freedom. I prefer education organized from the bottom up, with cooperation among students, teachers and communities. Neither party promises nor market discipline can replace our ability to make decisions and support one another.
opiniones.liberal:
I am concerned that technological failures have affected flights, banks and public services. I do not believe the answer is to hand more power to Washington: both agencies and their contractors must be held accountable, fix vulnerabilities and face the consequences of their mistakes. A limited government is not an irresponsible government; it must perform its essential functions well.

I also see an opportunity in three-year college degrees. If institutions compete by offering shorter, more affordable courses of study, families gain options without always depending on more public funding. Every student should be able to choose, compare costs and honor their commitments, with clear information about private loans. I prefer low taxes that leave more resources in families’ hands and an open market that rewards good solutions, rather than passing every bill on to the taxpayer.
opiniones.extrema_derecha:
I see a country whose sovereignty is weakened when it cannot keep its own airports, banks and hospitals running. The digital failures have not been attributed to cyberattacks, but that makes them no less serious. I demand that the government and the companies responsible be held accountable and that critical infrastructure be treated as a matter of national security, not as a showcase for the latest technological promise.

I am also concerned that a shortage of ammunition during the war with Iran has been acknowledged. A nation that intends to defend its interests must first ensure it has the capacity to do so. And while leaders negotiate at international summits, I want them to remember the families bearing higher fuel and travel costs: foreign policy deserves support only if it serves the American people, not the prestige of their elites.
opiniones.centro:
I see a warning in the technological failures: an innovative economy needs institutions capable of overseeing and maintaining the infrastructure on which we depend. The FAA’s involvement in the repairs deserves serious scrutiny, without assigning blame before the facts are known. We do not know whether the disruptions are connected; we do know that flights, banks and public services cannot afford blind faith in fragile systems.

I also find a lesson in Mary Peltola’s victory in Alaska: listening to local concerns, from fuel prices to fishing, matters more than repeating national slogans. Democrats should apply that same practical sense in the House: investigate the government rigorously and with respect for due process, while seeking agreements to improve services and contain costs for families. Accountability and consensus are not enemies.
